text.text: Your rentals in one place. Check Bookings arriving today and this week, make sure every Turnover has a cleaner, and keep Issues from reaching guests. Operational tracking only.
The cleaning between guests decides the next review. A written routine and a photo check make every home look the same every time.
Every check-out gets a turnover the moment the booking is confirmed (
Same-day turns (one guest leaves at 10, the next arrives at 4) go to your most reliable cleaner first.
Confirm with the cleaner 48 hours ahead and press
Strip and wash all linens and towels; make beds with fresh sets
Kitchen: dishes done, fridge emptied, counters and appliances wiped
Bathrooms scrubbed; hair checked on every surface
Floors vacuumed and mopped; under beds checked
Trash out, recycling sorted, bins back
Restock: toilet paper, soap, shampoo, coffee, dish soap, trash bags; tick
Thermostat set, lights off, doors and windows locked
Photos of every room sent to the host
Anything broken or stained goes in
with photos, and becomes an issue if it needs fixing.
Lost items are bagged and labeled with the booking. Message the guest the same day.
Damage claims through booking sites have short deadlines, often 14 days. Log it today.
Once a month, the host visits right after a clean and compares it with the photos. Feedback goes to the cleaner kindly and specifically.
Pay per turnover at an agreed rate, with extra for deep cleans and same-day turns. Record the cost on the turnover page so you know the true cost of each stay.
The family with a dog left six days ago. The cleaner restocked the house and noted extra dog hair in the living room, so the host adds a lint-roller to the supply list and a pet fee to the listing.

When one guest leaves at 10 and the next arrives at 4, send two cleaners or start the linens from a spare set so the beds are made by noon. Tell the arriving guest early check-in is not possible on those days.
Clear, warm messages at the right moments prevent most problems and most bad reviews. Write them once, then adjust for each guest.

text.text: How many guests, including children and pets?
Arrival time, so the home is ready and the code works.
Anything special: a birthday, a work trip, mobility needs.
. A party larger than the listing allows is a no.
Quiet hours, no parties, smoking, pets, maximum guests, parking. Keep them short and say why ("our neighbors are early risers"). Point to local rules where your permit requires it.
Reply within 15 minutes during the day, one hour at night.
Say what you will do and when: "Wade will be there by 2 pm to fix the shower."
Log the issue as Guest-impacting and follow up after the fix.
Offer a fair gesture if the problem affected the stay; it often saves the review.
Guests who booked directly or have stayed before are your most valuable. Send them a personal note and, when you can, first choice of dates for next season.
The anniversary couple arrives at the condo this week. The host's three-day message mentions the sunset view from the balcony and offers to leave a bottle of sparkling water in the fridge.
Never move a conversation or payment off a booking site's system when its rules forbid it.
Never share door codes before the guest's identity and booking are confirmed.
Things break in rentals more often than in homes, because so many people use them. Triage by whether a guest is affected, fix fast, and keep the history.

Before the next stay or two

text.text: Safety items, such as railings, smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors, are never routine.
Add the issue with the rental, priority, the date reported and who is fixing it.
Attach the guest's or cleaner's photos.
A small toolkit in every home

Spare batteries, light bulbs, a plunger, a basic tool set, router reset instructions, the breaker panel labeled, and the water shut-off tagged. Most guest-impacting issues can be solved in minutes with these.
Keep a handyman, a plumber, an electrician and a locksmith for each area, with after-hours numbers. Note on each rental page who to call first.
on every issue. At year end, issues by rental show which home is wearing out and what to budget for.

The beach house's outdoor shower runs hot only and was reported by the cleaner. It is not inside the house, but the family staying there uses it every day, so it is marked Guest-impacting and Wade is booked for this afternoon.
Tell the guest it is fixed and thank them for reporting it. Guests who see a quick fix often mention it in their review.
When the same issue appears three times in a season on one home, stop patching it. Replace the part or the appliance and record the cost, so guests stop meeting the problem.
Twice a year, each home gets a deeper look. It keeps reviews high, prevents expensive repairs, and sets prices for the season ahead.
Deep clean: windows, upholstery, carpets, behind appliances
Replace worn towels, sheets and pillows; count sets (three per bed is a good minimum)
Test smoke and carbon monoxide detectors; replace batteries
Service heating or cooling; clean filters
Check the outdoor areas: deck boards, railings, grill, outdoor furniture
Refresh listing photos if anything changed
Rental permit and insurance renewal dates checked
Look at last year's bookings by month: nights booked, average nightly rate and payout.
Raise prices for dates that booked far ahead last year; lower them where gaps stayed open.
Set minimum nights higher on weekends and holidays, lower in shoulder weeks.
Winterize what needs it: outdoor taps, hoses, pool or hot tub
Plan bigger repairs and upgrades for the empty weeks
Review the year: payouts earned per home, cleaning and repair costs, reviews
Lodging taxes filed for each period your area requires; totals come from
Keep receipts for repairs and supplies for your accountant.
The garden guest suite is paused for maintenance while the ceiling is repainted. The host uses the quiet weeks to refresh the photos and raise the summer rate before taking it live again.
At the end of each season, write three lines on this page: what guests loved, what they complained about, and one change for next season.

Before each season, count spare linens, towels, kitchen basics and cleaning stock in each home. Order what is short a month ahead so busy weeks never wait on a delivery. Record the count on this page so next season starts from real numbers instead of memory.

The back office for a host with a few homes: who is arriving and leaving, which cleanings are booked, what is broken, and what each home earned. The booking sites stay where guests book; this is where you run the operation across all of them.
: each home with permit number, nightly rate, minimum nights, status, usual cleaner, upcoming and current stays, and payouts earned.
: guest party, size, check-in and check-out, nights, channel, status, payout, cleaning fee and lodging tax.
: every cleaning between stays, the cleaner, the date, whether supplies were restocked and any damage found.
: repairs and problems, with priority, cost and who is fixing them.
